technique: the turn — the exact line where picture becomes meaning, and how the poem earns it
lesson: Today we learn one move: the turn. The turn is the exact line where a poem stops describing a thing and starts telling you what it means. For most of this poem, you get a stove door and a morning. Then the line changes. It says "You've spent a long day chasing numbers down their holes." That moves from the stove to your actual life. Then "let this be the hour the work has weight you can lift." Then at the end, "rise and meet it." That is the poem telling you plainly what to do. It works because the poem earned your trust with the stove and the ash first. By the time it speaks to you directly, you are already paying attention, so the instruction lands. Try this: describe one thing for several lines, then in one line say what it means to you. The second time through, listen for the exact line where the stove stops and your life starts. Here is the poem.
poem:
The handle of the stove door has worn smooth
where your palm meets it, iron gone the color
of river stone, and you know its give before it gives—
the little resistance, then the swing, then the ash
to be raked back and the kindling laid crosswise.
Cold mornings teach a man to be exact with small things,
to tend the one latch that must catch, to let the rest
rattle loose until he gets to them. Outside, the hills
hold their gray the way a kettle holds its waiting.
You've spent a long day chasing numbers down their holes;
let this be the hour the work has weight you can lift.
The light comes slow and honest over the near field.

The day you built waits for your hands—
rise and meet it.
